draft.title: Determinants and inverses
card: The inverse of a square matrix A is written A⁻¹. Multiplying A by A⁻¹ gives the identity matrix, so the inverse undoes what A did.
for A = [a b; c d], det A = ad − bc. Multiply the main diagonal, then subtract the product of the other diagonal.
if det A = 0, A has no inverse. If det A is not 0, A has an inverse.
draft.remember: Work out ad − bc. If it is 0 there is no inverse. If not, there is one.

a.q: For the matrix [4 3; 2 1], what is the determinant?
a.why: det = 4×1 − 3×2 = 4 − 6 = −2. Adding the products to get 10 is the tempting mistake, but the second product must be subtracted. Since −2 is not 0, this matrix has an inverse.
a.clue: Subtract the product of the other diagonal, 3 × 2.

b.q: For which value of k does the matrix [k 6; 2 3] have no inverse?
b.why: det = 3k − 6×2 = 3k − 12. No inverse needs det = 0, so 3k = 12 and k = 4. Setting k = 0 is tempting, but then det = −12, which is not 0, so an inverse exists.
b.clue: Set the determinant equal to 0 and solve for k.

final.title: Determinants and inverses
card: The inverse of a square matrix \(A\) is written \(A^{-1}\). Multiplying \(A\) by \(A^{-1}\) gives the identity matrix, so the inverse undoes what \(A\) did.
for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), \(\text{det}(A) = ad - bc\). Multiply the main diagonal, then subtract the product of the other diagonal.
if \(\text{det}(A) = 0\), \(A\) has no inverse. If \(\text{det}(A)\) is not 0, \(A\) has an inverse.
final.remember: Work out \(ad - bc\). If it is 0 there is no inverse. If not, there is one.

a.q: For the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), what is the determinant?
a.why: The determinant is \(4 \times 1 - 3 \times 2\), which is \(4 - 6 = -2\). Adding the products to get 10 is the tempting mistake, but the second product must be subtracted. Since \(-2\) is not 0, this matrix has an inverse.
a.clue: Subtract the product of the other diagonal, \(3 \times 2\).

b.q: For which value of \(k\) does the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} k & 6 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) have no inverse?
b.why: The determinant is \(3k - 6 \times 2 = 3k - 12\). No inverse needs a determinant of 0, so \(3k = 12\) and \(k = 4\). Setting \(k = 0\) is tempting, but then the determinant is \(-12\), which is not 0, so an inverse exists.
b.clue: Set the determinant equal to 0 and solve for \(k\).
